I am a layman when it comes to electrical engineering, physics, and ion propulsion. So I have what can be described as a dumb question:

Our air is a collection of inert gasses that resist ionization, making it a poor conductor and thus a poor fuel for an ion thruster. However in the few articles I have read the main problems presented in trying to use an ion thruster in an atmosphere are power concerns and atmospheric interference with the ionization process of the on-board fuel.

Now, being the ignorant layman I am, I have to ask: What happens in a situation where there is unlimited power? Lightning ionizes the air to create plasma... So if there is unlimited power sent to a thruster, could it use plain old air as the fuel, instead of Xenon, Argon, etc?
Ion thrusters and their use in a non-vacuum

I'm not sure, but I don't think adding more 'power' would help without redesigning the ion thruster.

As I understand it, ion thrusters accelerate particles using either electrostatic or electromagnetic forces. Simply throwing more electricity into a railgun won't necessarily make it work better. Eventually you'll just start arcing and melting things.

If you're asking 'can an ion thruster work in atmosphere' then I believe the answer is yes. If you're asking 'can an ion thruster make significantly more thrust by adding more electricity' then it's probably also yes. But I don't think an ion thruster will ever be the 'best' engine for the job, in a situation where you have atmosphere.

They are efficient and useful in space where resources are scarce, but those same qualities make them less useful here on earth where we have access to more material. For example, a simple electric motor with a propeller would generate far more thrust using far less of that 'unlimited power', by moving a lot more atmosphere.

The instant I saw them, before I knew what I was doing my body had spun around and kicked the door shut, quickly locking the door due to the countless practice from... things that teenage boys do, requiring closed doors. I slumped down on the floor by my bed, thanking God that for once my less-than-average reflexes had not failed me.

There are fucking zombies in my house. Why the hell are you just sitting there on the floor? My mind remembered, and I jolted back up. Where my family had gone I didn't know – living my life meant waking up at 12, and living my family's lives meant going about their business without waiting for me.

Oh god, oh god, what if they're dead already, I thought to myself. I'm going to die, I just know it. I frantically searched the room, looking for anything to defend myself with. Knowing my luck and from the expertise of the many zombie shows I had watched, these zombies meant that whatever virus overtook them was the kind that removed the limiter that humans subconsciously placed on themselves to keep from destroying their own body. In short, these flesh-eating mongrels currently scratching away at my door would run until their legs fell off, and had strength beyond that of the average person. This door would not hold for long.

My search of the room yielded nothing. Damn it, I thought to myself. I wished I had been a weeaboo like Kyle. His room proudly displayed two katana and various replica swords from anime. As never-used as they were (and as useless as Kyle was), right at this moment I wished I was him. Finding only a screwdriver and – to my luck, a boxcutter – I tried to formulate my plan of escape.

My room sat located at the end of a long hallway on the third floor at the edge of the house. Jumping from my window would mean certain impalement on the metal fence down below. What the fuck, dad, what if there was a fire? Here I was, the undead coming to get me, and I was thinking about fire safety.

I quieted myself, holding my breath, and listened. It sounded like there were maybe only two at my door, though if they were here on the third floor I couldn't just discard the possibility that there would be even more on the second floor, much less the ground-level one.

My reflexes were slow, but my thinking was my strength. Following the plan that I laid out in my head beforehand, I opened the door forcefully. I was thankful that my dad was just about the world's shittiest handyman, because the door he "repaired" now opened outwards, allowing me to push them back as I opened the door. The scent of rot hit me like a truck, but the bandanna that I had tied over my face beforehand kept my gagging to a minimum.

Right away, I swung down the boxcutting knife forcefully, stabbing the nearest undead on the cheek and cutting away the mottled flesh. Fuck, I missed. Being one of the types with a pathetic amount of upper body strength, I had always focused on my legs and running, so it came as no surprise when I kicked away the undead and it landed backwards in a heap. As the other undead came closer, trying to claw at my face, I ducked down low and popped up so close that its arms couldn't reach me. With a fistful of hair, I steadied myself and plunged the knife straight into its eyesocket, pulling it out with a suction sound and scattering chunky blood across the hall.

The four-hour marathon of Jackie Chan movies must have had some sort of effect on me, because I threw the now dead undead at my previously failed victim, knocking it down shortly after it had just gotten up. I took no hesitation in running over and crushing its skull with my shoe. If my mom was still alive, she was going to hate having to clean all this up.

I bolted over to the hallway window, nearly tearing it off its hinges as I opened it. Thank god my mother had a terrible sense of aesthetic and had my father install a trellis for vines to grow on. It was when I was halfway down, on the second storey, that it hit me.

My father installed this trellis. Half-assed nails gave way as I fell back with the vines, my back slamming into the ground below, crushing my leg underneath me. Something stirred nearby, and the sight of an undead crawling out of my apparently broken kitchen window was enough to set me running, despite the ankle I had awkwardly broken my fall with.

I ran to the church across the street, not knowing where else to go. I'm just a normal guy; why is this happening? I needed someone to save me. "Only Jesus can save you," I imagined in the voice of Father Bennett, whose church doors I was now running to. Really, what am I thinking of at a time like this?

Though I wasn't overweight like Kyle, my physique was more of the round kind than the upside-down triangle, so my exhaustion and adrenaline were high as I sat down on the nearest church pew, where I thought it would be safest. That is, until a hand grabbed my leg. That too, I stomped into oblivion with my good foot, as I stormed to the nearest stairs, tripping along the way and dropping my boxcutter. Of all the times to be a fucking klutz, it had to be now.

As I climbed the rickety metal stairs of the church, I ascended the spiral as I took the screwdriver that I had put into my belt. It turned out it would pay off. While I was looking down at my belt, I slammed full-on into a body, though from the whiff I got, I knew it was no longer the body of a person. I was thankful that it seemed nobody else was around, because I screamed like a little girl as I indisciminately stabbed at the face of the undead, eventually pushing it over the thin metal railing, hearing it land with a satisfying crunch down on the old tile down below.

I reached the top of the belltower, overlooking most of the city. A haze filled my eyes, smoke and fire from the ground seemingly coming from every direction. The highways were filled with cars, stretching as far as I could see. But the worst part was this.

There were no helicopters. There were no people. The world was quiet, too quiet. My ears no longer ringing from the adrenaline, I noticed a gentle buzzing in my ear. It was then that I noticed it wasn't a buzzing – it was the collective groaning of every undead nearby. The city was filled with the undead, as far as I could see. Banging sounds and groaning began to sound from down below; the many heavy, clumsy footsteps that were making their way up to where I was.

I closed the metal doors that opened from the stairs, and waited to think of another brilliant plan to escape, but nothing came. I dropped to my knees in despair, and did all that I could do.

I cried, and I waited.
